sims.title: What c·v + d·w can reach
sims.intro: The two starting vectors are the robot's steps from §1.1: $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{w}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}$, and the sliders $c$ and $d$ say how many of each to run. The red arrow is $c\mathbf{v}+d\mathbf{w}$, drawn as $c\mathbf{v}$ first and then $d\mathbf{w}$ tip-to-tail — the picture of 'do this, then that'.
watch: The readout $v_1w_2-v_2w_1$ is the test from §1.2. While it is nonzero, the two dashed guide lines point in genuinely different directions and every point of the plane is within reach.

Change $c$ alone: the red tip slides along a line parallel to $\mathbf{v}$. Change $d$ alone and it slides parallel to $\mathbf{w}$. Two independent slides are exactly why two non-parallel vectors cover a two-dimensional plane.
Setting $c=d=0$ lands on the origin. That is why the zero vector is on every plane described as $c\mathbf{v}+d\mathbf{w}$ — a question worth two marks on Midterm 2024.

challenges.prompt: With the starting vectors $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{w}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}$ in place, set $c=2$ and $d=4$ — the answer to the robot problem in §1.3. Read the sum.
challenges.explain: The readout shows $(14, 8)$: two of Step A and four of Step B land exactly on the target. Because $v_1w_2-v_2w_1 = -5 \ne 0$, Fact 1 promised in advance both that a recipe exists and that this is the only one — no other pair $(c,d)$ produces $(14,8)$.

challenges.prompt: Now make $\mathbf{w}$ a multiple of $\mathbf{v}$: leave $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$ and set $w_1=2$ and $w_2=4$, so $\mathbf{w}=2\mathbf{v}$. Then move $c$ and $d$ anywhere you like.
challenges.explain: The cross term drops to zero and the verdict changes to 'one line only'. Every combination now reads as a point on the line through $(1,2)$, whatever $c$ and $d$ do — because $c\mathbf{v}+d(2\mathbf{v}) = (c+2d)\mathbf{v}$. This is the trap in §1.2: two directions that are secretly one direction buy you no more reach than a single vector.

challenges.prompt: Keeping $\mathbf{w}=2\mathbf{v}$, try to reach the point $(14,8)$ by moving $c$ and $d$: start with $c=5$ and $d=1$, then try any other pair.
challenges.explain: It cannot be done, and the readout shows why: every sum has its second component exactly twice the first, while $(14,8)$ has $8 \ne 28$. The algebraic version of the same fact is the contradiction $2\times 14 \ne 8$ between the two component equations — which is what you would write in an exam answer.

sims.title: The dot product, the angle, and the right-angle test
sims.intro: Six readouts, in the order an exam answer works through them: the dot product, then the two lengths, then $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|\|\mathbf{w}\|}$, then $\theta$ itself. If your hand calculation disagrees with the final angle, comparing line by line tells you which step slipped.
watch: The sign of $\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w}$ tracks the angle exactly: positive under $90°$, zero at $90°$, negative above it. That is Theorem 1 doing its work, since $\cos\theta$ is the only factor on the right that can change sign.

Lengthen $\mathbf{v}$ without turning it (set it to $(1,2)$, then to $(2,4)$): the dot product doubles but $\theta$ does not move. Dividing by both lengths is what removes the size and leaves the direction.
$\cos\theta$ never leaves $[-1,1]$, however extreme the components get. That is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality showing up as a guarantee that $\arccos$ always has an answer.

challenges.prompt: Set $\mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\-3\end{bmatrix}$ against the starting $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}$, and read the dot product and the angle.
challenges.explain: $\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w} = 12-12 = 0$ and $\theta = 90°$: this is the swap-and-negate construction from §1.7, where the cancellation is forced by the algebra rather than by these particular numbers. Note both vectors have length 5 and neither is zero — a zero dot product says nothing about either vector being zero.

challenges.prompt: Now set $\mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix}-3\\-4\end{bmatrix}$, the exact reverse of the unchanged $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}$.
challenges.explain: $\theta = 180°$ and $\cos\theta = -1$, so $\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w} = -\|\mathbf{v}\|\|\mathbf{w}\| = -25$ — as negative as it is possible to get for these two lengths. Opposite directions are the extreme case of a negative dot product, not a case of zero.

challenges.prompt: Set $\mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$, still against $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}$, and compute $\cos\theta$ by hand before reading it off.
challenges.explain: $\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w} = 3+8 = 11$, $\|\mathbf{v}\| = 5$, $\|\mathbf{w}\| = \sqrt5$, so $\cos\theta = \dfrac{11}{5\sqrt5} \approx 0.984$ and $\theta \approx 10.3°$. The two directions are close but not identical — and the check that catches a slip is that $\cos\theta$ came out inside $[-1,1]$.

sims.title: Ax: the same answer by columns and by rows
sims.intro: The thin arrows are the columns $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ of $A$ — fixed directions stored once. The dashed arrows are $x_1\mathbf{a}_1$ then $x_2\mathbf{a}_2$, laid tip-to-tail, and the red arrow is $A\mathbf{x}$. The last three readouts recompute the same product row by row.
watch: 'Ax by columns' and the two row readouts always match. That is Theorem 2, and it is the free check you should run on every product you compute by hand.
Changing $\mathbf{x}$ moves the red arrow but leaves the thin column arrows alone: $\mathbf{x}$ is the recipe, $A$ is the pair of ingredients.

Make the two columns parallel — $\mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}2\\4\end{bmatrix}$ — and every $A\mathbf{x}$ is trapped on one line, whatever $\mathbf{x}$ is. The reachable outputs of a matrix are exactly the combinations of its columns.

challenges.prompt: With the starting $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, set $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix}$ and confirm both routes agree.
challenges.explain: Columns: $4\begin{bmatrix}2\\0\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}10\\6\end{bmatrix}$. Rows: $2(4)+1(2) = 10$ and $0(4)+3(2) = 6$. Identical, as Theorem 2 requires — and if your own two computations ever disagree, one of them contains an arithmetic slip, not a conceptual one.

challenges.prompt: Set $x_1 = 1$ and $x_2 = 0$. Where does the red arrow land, and why?
challenges.explain: On column 1 exactly: $A\mathbf{x} = 1\mathbf{a}_1+0\mathbf{a}_2 = \mathbf{a}_1$. Feeding in a vector with a single 1 selects that column — which is why the columns of $A$ are the natural things to think in, and why the identity matrix (Module 02) selects every column and changes nothing.

challenges.prompt: Make the columns parallel: $a_{11}=1$, $a_{21}=2$, $a_{12}=2$, $a_{22}=4$. Then move $\mathbf{x}$ around.
challenges.explain: Every output lands on the line through $(1,2)$, because $A\mathbf{x} = (x_1+2x_2)\mathbf{a}_1$. Most target vectors $\mathbf{b}$ are therefore unreachable, so $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has no solution for them — the same collapse you met in §1.2, now stated about a matrix. Module 02 gives it a name: this $A$ is singular.
